claim: Human thymidylate synthase (hTS) is an obligate, stable homodimer with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 80 nM.
source: Human thymidylate synthase (hTS) is an obligate, stable homodimer (Kd = 80 nM Genovese et al., 2010) with two active sites, each including residues from both monomers (Costi et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Genovese et al., 2010, which provides the Kd value.

claim: hTS has two active sites, each including residues from both monomers.
source: Human thymidylate synthase (hTS) is an obligate, stable homodimer (Kd = 80 nM Genovese et al., 2010) with two active sites, each including residues from both monomers (Costi et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Costi et al., 2005.

claim: hTS catalyzes the reductive methylation of deoxyuridylate (dUMP) to dTMP using methylenetetrahydrofolate (mTHF) as the one-carbon methyl donor.
source: As a dimeric enzyme, it provides the sole de novo pathway to deoxythymidylate (dTMP) synthesis in human cells by catalyzing the reductive methylation of deoxyuridylate (dUMP) to dTMP using methylenetetrahydrofolate (mTHF) as the one-carbon methyl donor (Costi et al., 2005; Carreras and Santi, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Costi et al., 2005 and Carreras and Santi, 1995.

claim: hTS provides the sole de novo pathway to deoxythymidylate (dTMP) synthesis in human cells.
source: As a dimeric enzyme, it provides the sole de novo pathway to deoxythymidylate (dTMP) synthesis in human cells by catalyzing the reductive methylation of deoxyuridylate (dUMP) to dTMP using methylenetetrahydrofolate (mTHF) as the one-carbon methyl donor (Costi et al., 2005; Carreras and Santi, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Costi et al., 2005 and Carreras and Santi, 1995.

claim: hTS regulates its own levels and those of other proteins involved in apoptotic processes, including bcl2, c-myc, and p53, by interacting with its own and other mRNAs.
source: By interacting with its own and other mRNAs, this protein regulates its own levels and those of other proteins involved in apoptotic processes, including bcl2, c-myc, and p53 (Brunn et al., 2014; Jennings and Willis, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brunn et al., 2014 and Jennings and Willis, 2015.

claim: Classical hTS inhibitors such as 5-fluorodeoxyuridine 5'-monophosphate (FdUMP) compete with the dUMP substrate.
source: Its inhibition is usually achieved with compounds that bind at the protein active-site, competing either with the dUMP substrate, such as 5-fluorodeoxyurdine 5'-monophosphate (FdUMP), or with the folate cofactor, such as raltitrexed (RTX) and pemetrexed (PMX) (Carreras and Santi, 1995; Jennings and Willis, 2015; Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carreras and Santi, 1995 and Jennings and Willis, 2015.

claim: Classical hTS inhibitors such as raltitrexed (RTX) and pemetrexed (PMX) compete with the folate cofactor.
source: Its inhibition is usually achieved with compounds that bind at the protein active-site, competing either with the dUMP substrate, such as 5-fluorodeoxyurdine 5'-monophosphate (FdUMP), or with the folate cofactor, such as raltitrexed (RTX) and pemetrexed (PMX) (Carreras and Santi, 1995; Jennings and Willis, 2015; Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carreras and Santi, 1995 and Jennings and Willis, 2015.

claim: Classical hTS inhibitors induce cells to develop drug resistance associated with increased hTS levels which eventually leads to therapy failure.
source: However, these drugs induce cells to develop drug resistance associated with increased hTS levels which eventually leads to therapy failure (Peters, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peters, 2018.

claim: The Y202 pocket of hTS accommodates the side chain of F59' from the other monomer.
source: We selected the 'Y202 pocket', which accommodates the side chain of F59' from the other monomer, as the most promising region to target (Figure 1C–F, Figure 2A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Salo-Ahen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Salo-Ahen et al., 2015 and references to figures showing the structural details.

claim: The hTS C195S-Y202C double mutant was inactive but takes the active conformation of hTS.
source: As expected from removal of the catalytic C195 residue, this double mutant was inactive, but X-ray crystallography showed that it takes the active conformation of hTS (Figure 1F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data presented in figures and supplementary files.

claim: Compounds A5, A10, A20, and TPC were selected through tethering experiments and bound to cysteine-containing peptides of hTS.
source: Four molecules, A5, A10, A20, and TPC also bound peptide (D186-R215) DLPLMALPPSHALCQFCVVNSELSCQLYQR (sequence C) (Supplementary file 3C), containing the engineered Y202C together with the native C199 and C210.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data reported in Supplementary file 3C.

claim: Compound B12 caused a decrease in FRET efficiency (ΔΦFRET = -0.13).
source: Among the 26 compounds selected by VS, B12 and B26 (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 4A), caused low but reproducible decreases in the efficiency of FRET (ΔΦFRET = -0.13 and ΔΦFRET = -0.02, respectively), thus indicating some ability to perturb the enzyme dimeric assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET assay data.

claim: Compound B26 caused a decrease in FRET efficiency (ΔΦFRET = -0.02).
source: Among the 26 compounds selected by VS, B12 and B26 (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 4A), caused low but reproducible decreases in the efficiency of FRET (ΔΦFRET = -0.13 and ΔΦFRET = -0.02, respectively), thus indicating some ability to perturb the enzyme dimeric assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET assay data.

claim: Compounds C2, C3, and C4 featured IC50 values of 5.25, 83, and 246 μM against 300 nM hTS, respectively.
source: The former three, differing only for the position of the carboxylic group on the phenyl ring, featured IC50 values 5.25, 83 and 246 μM vs. 300 nM hTS (Supplementary file 4) and were selected for a quantitative mechanistic analysis of FRET and inhibition data with recombinant hTS (see the next paragraph).
evidence: The claim is supported by IC50 measurements reported in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Compounds E5, E6, and E7 featured IC50 values against 300 nM recombinant hTS of 40, 10, and 7 μM, respectively.
source: It was however compounds E5, E6, and E7 that proved to be the most interesting to continue our study. They featured IC50 values against 300 nM recombinant hTS of 40, 10 and 7 μM respectively, and decreased FRET efficiency by –0.24 at 50 μM (E5, E6) and –0.1 at 10 μM (E7, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by IC50 measurements reported in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Compound E7 is a racemic mixture of two enantiomers that equilibrated with a half-life of 56 min.
source: Compound E7, that was the most active on cells, was determined to be a racemic mixture of two enantiomers that equilibrated with a half-life of 56 min (Appendix 3, Appendix 3—figure 1, Appendix 3—figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Appendix 3.

claim: Compound C3 co-elutes with hTS dimers and monomers in anion-exchange chromatography.
source: Co-elution, hence stable non covalent binding of the C3 inhibitor with hTS, was established by the observation that the fractions containing the hTS dimers and monomers also exhibited absorption at 350 nm (Figure 3E), a wavelength at which no absorption comes from the protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by anion-exchange chromatography data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Compound C3 has a higher affinity for hTS monomers than for dimers.
source: This finding suggests a somewhat larger affinity of the ligand for the latter. Consistently, parallel MS experiments in which 4 μM E5 was loaded on the AE column with hTS identified this ligand mainly in the fractions containing the protein monomers (see additional information in the Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data reported in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Binding of compounds C2-C4 to hTS causes a fivefold increase in the equilibrium dissociation constant for the protein.
source: As expected for a dissociative inhibition mechanism, the limit values of ΦFRET at high C3 concentrations were consistent with a 5-fold increase in the equilibrium dissociation constant for the protein bound to C3 with respect to the free protein (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Compound C3 has a higher affinity for hTS monomers (KI = 10^-6 M) than for dimers (KI' = 1.7 x 10^-5 M).
source: This finding is supported by the higher affinities of the inhibitors for the hTS monomer (KI = 10–6 M) than for the dimer (KI'=1.7 x 10–5 M), as obtained by fitting of the FRET data in Figure 4B.
evidence: The claim is supported by fitting of FRET data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Compound E5-FITC proved slightly less active at inhibiting recombinant hTS than E5 (IC50s = 40 and 100 μM, respectively).
source: It proved slightly less active at inhibiting recombinant hTS than E5 (IC50s=40 and 100 μM, for E5 and E5-FITC, respectively), likely because the probe tail caused some steric hindrance for its binding to the enzyme.
evidence: The claim is supported by IC50 measurements.

claim: Cells expressing TC-TS produced a significantly higher average FRET signal (4222±2128) than control cells expressing WT TS (1250±1178), proving intracellular hTS/E5 engagement.
source: Indeed, our image analysis (Figure 5) showed that cells expressing TC-TS produced a significantly higher (Ρ<0.0001) average FRET signal (4222±2128) than control cells that expressed WT TS (1250±1178), thus proving the occurrence of intracellular hTS/E5 engagement.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: E7 was almost equally active against both PDAC2 and PDAC5 cells, which were sensitive to 5-FU.
source: Noteworthy, E7 was almost as equally active against both PDAC2 and PDAC5 cells. Both were sensitive to 5-FU (Supplementary file 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth inhibition data reported in Supplementary file 6A.

claim: The LPc167 primary culture, which expressed high levels of TS, was resistant to 5-FU but still sensitive to E7.
source: The LPc167 primary culture, which expressed high levels of TS was resistant to 5-FU but still sensitive to E7 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell growth inhibition data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: E7 was the most interesting compound, being active on all the cancer cells tested with IC50 values between 10 and 37 µM after 72 hr of exposure.
source: E7 was the most interesting among these compounds, being active on all the cancer cells tested with IC50 values between 10 and 37 µM after 72 hr of exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by IC50 measurements on various cancer cell lines.

claim: E7 induced apoptotic death in A2780 and A2780/CP cells after a 48 hr treatment with a slightly higher efficiency than PMX.
source: Remarkably, E7 induced apoptotic death in the two cell lines after a 48 hr treatment with a slightly higher efficiency than PMX (Figure 6B and C, , Figure 7—figure supplement 1 , Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Treatment of A2780 and A2780/CP cells with E5 and E7 caused a dose-dependent decrease in hTS protein levels.
source: Following treatment of both A2780 and A2780/CP cells with E5 and E7, while we found no change in the levels of the DHFR protein, the level of the hTS protein decreased significantly in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Treatment with PMX and 5-FU increased hTS protein levels in A2780 and A2780/CP cells.
source: In the same cell lines, we observed increased levels of hTS after treatment with both PMX and 5-FU (Figure 7B ).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The half-life of hTS was 3 hr in untreated A2780 cancer cells.
source: As shown in Figure 7C, we found that the half-life of hTS was 3 hr in untreated cancer cells and that the degradation rate of the enzyme increased by 20% in E7–treated A2780 cell (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The degradation rate of hTS increased by 20% in E7-treated A2780 cells.
source: As shown in Figure 7C, we found that the half-life of hTS was 3 hr in untreated cancer cells and that the degradation rate of the enzyme increased by 20% in E7–treated A2780 cell (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The proteasome inhibitor MG132 restored hTS levels in E7-treated A2780 cells.
source: Indeed, as shown in Figure 7E, MG132 restored the hTS levels in treated cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: E5 and E7 reduced the catalytic activity of hTS by 25-30% in cellular extracts of A2780, A2780/CP, 2008, and C13* cell lines.
source: In these conditions, the catalytic activity of hTS was systematically reduced by 25–30% in the cellular extracts of all cell lines (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with E7 caused a significant decrease of the hTS dimer/monomer ratio relative to the control (-40 ± 10%).
source: The treatment caused a significant decrease of the dimer/monomer ratio relative to the control (- 40 ± 10%, Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-linking experiments shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The monomeric hTS F59A variant is unstable and undergoes much faster turnover than the dimeric WT protein.
source: As for the proteins, the F59A variant was already hardly discernible at time 0 (24 hrs after ectopic expression) while the dimeric WT hTS showed a turnover of about 8.5 hr. Thus, the monomeric hTSF59A variant is unstable and undergoes much faster turnover than the dimeric WT protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase experiments on HCT116 cells expressing WT hTS or hTS F59A mutant.

claim: E7 reached its tmax value after about 5 min with plasma levels in the micromolar range after both i.v. and oral administration in mice.
source: E7 showed the best PK profile (Figure 8A). Both after i.v. and oral administration it reached its tmax value after about 5 min with plasma levels in the micromolar range, i.e. concentrations that had caused a cell-growth inhibition in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacokinetic data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: E7 has a half-life of 13.6 hr in mice.
source: With a half-life of 13.6 hr, a prolonged exposure of the target tissue to the drug is expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacokinetic data.

claim: The mean G-luc signal was significantly lower in mice treated with E7 compared with control mice (46183±2015 vs 67905±6159 RLU/sec at day 25; p=0.001).
source: This mean signal was significantly lower in mice treated with E7 compared with control mice (46183±2015 vs 67905±6159 RLU/sec at day 25; p=0.001, two-sided t test).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioluminescence imaging data from the orthotopic PDAC model.

claim: Starting from day 30, the group receiving E7 had significantly lower G-luc intensity compared with mice receiving 5-FU (at day 30, -70% and -48%, relative to control mice, respectively).
source: Moreover, starting from day 30, the group receiving E7 had significantly lower G-luc intensity compared with mice receiving 5-FU (i.e., at day 30,–70% and –48%, relative to control mice, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioluminescence imaging data from the orthotopic PDAC model.

claim: Mice treated with E7 had significantly longer survival compared with control mice (P=0.03).
source: Tumor growth inhibition was reflected in a significantly longer survival of mice treated with E7 as compared with control mice (P=0.03, Figure 8E) and 5-FU (58 days, 43.3 days, and 50 days, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: E7 treatment led to a reduced expression of TS mRNA, down to 40-50% of the reference level in tumor tissues from the PDAC orthotopic model.
source: Conversely, E7 treatment led to a reduced expression of TS mRNA, down to 40–50% of the reference level (Figure 8F) in complete agreement with the results obtained with model cancer cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2 ).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: E7 caused a decrease in the levels of hTS protein that was more pronounced than 5-FU in tumor tissues from the PDAC orthotopic model.
source: Immunohistochemistry staining showed that E7 caused a decrease in the levels of hTS protein that was even more pronounced than 5-FU (Figure 8G). The hTS protein levels measured with the histological score (H-score) was 48±5 a.u. for E7 vs. 242±26 a.u. for 5-FU (p<0.001, two-sided t test).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: E7 reduced the proliferation of cancer cells, as detected by the reduced number of Ki67-positive cells.
source: Additional analyses showed that E7 reduced the proliferation of the cancer cells, as detected by the reduced number of Ki67-positive cells, while increasing apoptotic cell death, as assessed by the staining of cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: E7 increased apoptotic cell death, as assessed by the staining of cleaved caspase-3.
source: Additional analyses showed that E7 reduced the proliferation of the cancer cells, as detected by the reduced number of Ki67-positive cells, while increasing apoptotic cell death, as assessed by the staining of cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: E7 caused a significant reduction of tumor growth compared with control mice in the A2780 xenograft model (596.1±167.7 vs 2319.9±289.7 mm3 at day 6; 776.5±191.6 vs 3102.0±516.2 mm3 at day 7; p<0.05).
source: We found that also in this model, E7 caused a significant reduction of tumor growth compared with control mice (596.1±167.7 vs 2319.9±289.7 mm3 at day 6; 776.5±191.6 vs 3102.0±516.2 mm3 at day 7; p<0.05, two-sided t test), which was confirmed by quantification of the area under curve and resulted in significantly longer survival (p=0.0111; 24 days vs 16 days; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor volume measurements shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increased TS expression is a result of the common mechanisms of 5-FU resistance.
source: Numerous reports have shown that increased TS expression is a result of the common mechanisms of 5-FU resistance (Longley et al., 2003; Iijchi K et al, 2014; Vodenkova S et al, 2020; Ahn et al., 2015; Aschele C et al, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: 5-FU induces cytotoxicity by either inhibiting the action of thymidylate synthase (TS) or misincorporating its metabolites into RNA and DNA.
source: 5-FU induces cytotoxicity either by interfering with essential biosynthetic activities, namely, by either inhibiting the action of thymidylate synthase (TS) or misincorporating its metabolites into RNA and DNA (Sethy C and Kundu CN, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sethy C and Kundu CN, 2021.

claim: Formation of the stable enzyme dimer-substrate-inhibitor complex with 5-FU leads to prolonged engagement of the enzyme by the drug and eventually to thymineless cell death.
source: Formation of this stable complex leads to prolonged engagement of the enzyme by the drug and, eventually, to thymineless cell death.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about 5-FU mechanism of action.

claim: Formation of the stable enzyme dimer-substrate-inhibitor complex with 5-FU induces translational derepression of TS-mRNA and results in enzyme up-regulation, accounting for the occurrence of 5-FU resistance.
source: However, it also induces translational derepression of TS-mRNA and results in the enzyme up-regulation, accounting for the occurrence of 5-FU resistance (Chu and Allegra, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chu and Allegra, 1996.

claim: Enzyme stabilization has been indicated as an important primary mechanism of TS induction by fluoropyrimidines.
source: Additionally, enzyme stabilization has been indicated as an important primary mechanism of TS induction by fluoropyrimidines (Kitchens et al., 1999a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kitchens et al., 1999a.

claim: TS turnover is carried out in an ubiquitin-independent manner.
source: TS turnover is carried out in an ubiquitin-independent manner (Forsthoefel et al., 2004; Peña et al., 2006) and FdUMP binding to the TS protein leads to dramatic conformational changes which account for a stabilization of the enzyme and an increase in its half-life and intracellular levels (Kitchens et al., 1999b; Marverti et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Forsthoefel et al., 2004 and Peña et al., 2006.

claim: FdUMP binding to the TS protein leads to dramatic conformational changes which account for a stabilization of the enzyme and an increase in its half-life and intracellular levels.
source: TS turnover is carried out in an ubiquitin-independent manner (Forsthoefel et al., 2004; Peña et al., 2006) and FdUMP binding to the TS protein leads to dramatic conformational changes which account for a stabilization of the enzyme and an increase in its half-life and intracellular levels (Kitchens et al., 1999b; Marverti et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kitchens et al., 1999b and Marverti et al., 2009.

claim: The Y202 pocket is large enough (22 Å3) to accommodate a phenyl group and has several smaller crevices around it.
source: It is large enough (22 Å3) to accommodate a phenyl group and has several smaller crevices around it.
evidence: The claim is based on computational analysis of the Y202 pocket.

claim: During MD simulations of monomeric hTS, the side chain of Y202 moved away leaving a larger pocket and behaving like a gate.
source: During the MD simulations of monomeric hTS, the side chain of Y202 moved away leaving a larger pocket and behaving like a gate.
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The hTS C195S-Y202C double mutant crystallized in the space group P212121 with four independent subunits in the ASU, all in the active conformation.
source: The hTS C195S-Y202C crystallized in the space group P212121with four independent subunits in the ASU, all in the active conformation.
evidence: The claim is based on X-ray crystallography data.

claim: The hTS-C195S-Y202C structure is the first example of hTS crystallized in the active conformation under high salt conditions.
source: The hTS-C195S-Y202C structure is the first example of hTS crystallized in the active conformation under high salt conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on X-ray crystallography data and comparison with previous structures.

claim: The shift of hTS towards the active conformation in the C195S-Y202C mutant seems due to the active site C195S mutation.
source: Since both mutants crystallized under the same conditions, the shift of hTS towards the active conformation seems due to the active site C195S mutation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from X-ray crystallography data comparing the two mutants.

claim: A possible explanation for the shift to active conformation is that the clustering of the four residues C180 and C195 from the two dimer subunits stabilizes the inactive conformation of hTS, thus the C195S mutation prevents this occurrence.
source: A possible explanation is that the clustering of the four residues C180 and C195 from the two dimer subunits stabilizes the inactive conformation of hTS, thus the C195S mutation prevents this occurrence.
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation based on structural observations.

claim: In both hTS-Y202C and hTS-C195S-Y202C structures, C202 is chemically modified to S,S-(2-hydroxyethyl)thiocysteine (CME).
source: In both structures, the Fourier difference map clearly shows the replacement of the native Y202 by cysteine. Moreover, a positive extra electron density is found extending beyond the cysteine sulfur atom strongly indicating its reaction with β-mercaptoethanol (BME) present in the crystallization solution. Thus, C202 is chemically modified to S,S-(2-hydroxyethyl)thiocysteine (CME) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b and c).
evidence: The claim is based on X-ray crystallography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The structure of hTS C195S-Y202C validates the choice of Y202 as tethering mutation site, showing that this residue is prone to react with thiol compounds independently of the enzyme conformation.
source: Thus, the structure of hTS C195S-Y202C validates the choice of Y202 as tethering mutation site, showing that this residue is prone to react with thiol compounds independently of the enzyme conformation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from X-ray crystallography data.

claim: C202 is located in a dimer interface pocket considered important for protein-protein interactions.
source: C202 is located in a dimer interface pocket considered important for protein-protein interactions.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis.

claim: In both hTS-Y202C and hTS-C195S-Y202C variants, the loop K47-T55 of the facing subunit is displaced with respect to the structure of wt-hTS, increasing the intersubunit distances by 1.0-2.5 Å.
source: In both variants, the loop K47-T55 of the facing subunit is displaced with respect to the structure of wt-hTS, increasing the intersubunit distances by 1.0–2.5 Å.
evidence: The claim is based on X-ray crystallography data comparing mutant and wild-type structures.

claim: Small-to-medium-sized molecules, such as BME or the LR octapeptide, can access the dimer interface of the enzyme.
source: As already suggested by the structure of wt-hTS in complex with the LR peptide (Cardinale et al., 2011), small-to-medium-sized molecules, such as BME or the LR octapeptide, can access the dimer interface of the enzyme.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cardinale et al., 2011 and structural observations.

claim: The hTS dimer undergoes either monomer/dimer interconversion or 'breathing' movements that allow the binding at the dimer interface of exogenous molecules.
source: Thus, the structural evidence indicates that the hTS dimer undergoes either monomer/dimer interconversion or 'breathing' movements that allow the binding at the dimer interface of exogenous molecules, such as disulfide fragments.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from structural data.

claim: The higher affinity of compound C3 for hTS relative to its isomers C2 and C4 is explained by the ability of the para carboxylic group of C3 to establish an additional H-bond with R175.
source: The reliability of our docking virtual experiments was strengthened by their ability to explain the observed higher affinity for hTS of compound C3 relative to its isomers, C2 and C4. While the nitro-groups of all these ligands can make head-to-head hydrogen-bonding interactions with R64 (Figure 3C–D), only the para carboxylic group of compound C3 arranges properly to establish an additional H-bond with R175. Instead, the meta and ortho carboxylic groups of C2 and C4 do not have the correct orientations for interacting with this arginine residue.
evidence: The claim is based on computational docking studies shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: When bound to the inhibitor C3, the dimeric enzyme is less catalytically active than when free.
source: This difference in the limit behaviors of v and ΦFRET suggests that, when bound to the inhibitor, the dimeric enzyme is less catalytically active than when free.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from kinetic and FRET data.

claim: The kinetic results confirm a progressive dissociation of the enzyme dimer to monomers upon subsequent additions of C3.
source: The latter is therefore confirmed to be both a dimer disrupter and a dissociative inhibitor, the two roles being intimately connected with each other.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of kinetic data.

claim: Compound C3 is both a dimer disrupter and a dissociative inhibitor.
source: The latter is therefore confirmed to be both a dimer disrupter and a dissociative inhibitor, the two roles being intimately connected with each other.
evidence: The claim is based on combined FRET and kinetic data analysis.

claim: The ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation pathway is an important mechanism to destroy destabilized proteins in cells, and hTS is one of the substrates of this pathway.
source: The ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation pathway is an important mechanism to destroy destabilized proteins in cells, and hTS is one of the substrates of this pathway (Peña et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peña et al., 2009.

claim: Previous reports on other cell models have shown that 5-FU causes a remarkable slowdown of the TS degradation rate because most of the protein is engaged in a ternary complex with the folate substrate and the inhibitor, being thus protected from the proteasome.
source: In fact, previous reports on other cell models have shown that 5-FU causes a remarkable slowdown of the TS degradation rate because most of the protein is engaged in a ternary complex with the folate substrate and the inhibitor, being thus protected from the proteasome (Berger et al., 2004; Peña et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2014; Kitchens et al., 1999a; Kitchens et al., 1999b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: E7 reduces the hTS levels in cancer cells by enhancing its proteasomal degradation.
source: Based on the above data, we conclude that E7 reduces the hTS levels in cancer cells by enhancing its proteasomal degradation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including cycloheximide chase and proteasome inhibitor experiments.

claim: The promotion of hTS proteasomal degradation in cells by E7 is due to an increased fraction of more labile monomers.
source: Because E7 behaves as a disrupter of the dimeric recombinant protein, we anticipate that the promotion of its proteasomal degradation in cells is due to an increased fraction of more labile monomers (Figure 7G).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from recombinant protein studies and cellular experiments.

claim: The hTS F59A variant has a Kd of 1.3x10^-4 M in buffer and is expected to be essentially monomeric at all physiological concentrations.
source: While WT, with its 60–80 nM Kd in buffer, is expected to be essentially dimeric at all physiological concentrations, the F59A variant, with a Kd of 1.3x10–4 M in buffer is, instead, expected to be essentially monomeric (Salo-Ahen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Salo-Ahen et al., 2015.

claim: The expressions of the mRNAs of WT hTS and F59A variant showed no statistically significant differences.
source: The expressions of the mRNAs of the two proteins showed no statistically significant differences (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The mice treated with 5-FU did not show a decrease in TS mRNA expression and showed a more intense staining for TS.
source: The mice treated with 5-FU did not show a decrease in TS mRNA expression and showed a more intense staining for TS, in agreement with earlier studies in which treatment with 5-FU had induced TS activity both in mice and patients (Van der Wilt et al., 1992; Peters et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and immunohistochemistry data, and citations to Van der Wilt et al., 1992 and Peters et al., 2002.

claim: These dimer destabilizers represent new, promising tools to fight drug resistance associated with high TS levels in different tumor types such as colorectal, ovarian, and pancreatic cancers.
